hops.title: Say it: a mayfly baby can wait years to fly
hops.text: "Some mayfly babies spend two or three years growing in the creek. Then they grow wings, and a grown-up mayfly may live for only about a day!" If your child spots three thin tails, look for tiny gills along the sides of its belly. See both clues? Try this line. It turns "just a bug" into a wait-what surprise.

sources.citation: Utah State University Extension, Swaner Preserve and EcoCenter: Mayfly

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A slender three-tailed mayfly nymph with small gills along its sides underwater near creek pebbles, with a winged adult mayfly hovering above the sunlit surface.
image.caption: Some mayflies spend two or three years underwater. An adult may live for only a day.

hops.title: Compare it: a caddisfly case is a sleeping bag you crawl around in
hops.text: Some caddisfly babies crawl around in what looks like a tiny sleeping bag. They glue twigs, sand grains or pebbles together and drag the case along the rocks. Some twig cases look like tiny log cabins. Ask your child what they would build their own creek camper from.

sources.citation: Utah State University Extension, Swaner Preserve and EcoCenter: Caddisfly
Missouri Department of Conservation, Field Guide: Caddisfly Larvae

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small caddisfly larva peeking out of a tube case built from tiny twigs, crawling on a creek rock.
image.caption: Some caddisfly babies make little houses from twigs, sand or pebbles and carry them as they crawl.

hops.title: Point at it: white splashes put air into the water
hops.text: Stay within arm's reach of your child on a firm, dry park path set back from the creek. Point to the white splashes where water tumbles over rocks. Then look at a smooth pool nearby. Notice all those tiny bubbles: tumbling water mixes oxygen from the air into the stream.

sources.citation: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, CADDIS: Dissolved Oxygen

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A parent and child seen from behind on a park path set back from a creek, the parent pointing at white bubbly water tumbling over rocks beside a calm pool.
image.caption: Water splashing over rocks mixes oxygen from the air into the creek.

audio.title: Three playful ways to talk about creek critters
audio.transcript: Hi there. Before you head out to the creek with your kitchen strainer and white tray, here are three fun ways to talk about what you find under the rocks. First, if your child spots three thin tails and little gills along the sides of the bug's belly, try telling them, "Some mayfly babies spend two or three years underwater. A winged adult may live for only about a day." Many mayfly babies crawl on rocks. See those little gills? They take in oxygen from the water. Sometimes years in the creek, and maybe just a day as a grown-up. That's a surprise in one tiny bug. Second, if you spot a tiny tube of twigs or sand grains that suddenly starts walking across the tray, compare it to a sleeping bag you crawl around in. Many caddisfly babies glue sticks, bits of plants or tiny pebbles into cases they carry as they crawl. Some twig cases look like tiny log cabins. Ask your child what they would build their own creek camper from. Third, when your child asks why many stonefly babies live in clean, flowing water, tell them that moving water brings them oxygen. When oxygen runs low, many stonefly babies do tiny push-ups to move fresh water over their bodies and gills. You can stand on dry grass a few steps back from the water and do two goofy push-ups together. Then point at the white splashes tumbling over the rocks. All that churning mixes oxygen from the air into the water. Have fun out there, stay within arm's reach, and put every critter gently back where you found it.
